extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy industry professionals (bookers, managers, club staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices used by a Comedy Cellar booker to evaluate comedians in five-minute auditions and construct nightly lineups; includes what disqualifies performers and how recommendations and clips factor into booking. Useful for comedians seeking club spots and industry professionals learning booking norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-minute audition window
rubrics_metrics.description: New comics get five minutes when they audition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estee forms an overall impression from that five-minute set; if she thinks 'there is something there' she gives a few regular spots and follows up. There is no formal pass system like at other clubs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and stage presence
rubrics_metrics.description: The booker watches for confidence and how the comic handles themselves on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She 'is in your face' at the door and expects performers to handle pressure. Lack of confidence or inability to manage stage presence in front of an engaged audience is a negative signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: How a comic handles a joke that doesn't land
rubrics_metrics.description: What happens when a joke bombs is considered the most important factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She looks for recovery, poise, and how the performer responds. Examples of poor responses (anti-patterns) include gestures or attitudes that belittle the audience or reveal arrogance; crying or visibly falling apart undermines the performer's prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding vulgar/bathroom jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathroom jokes are a disqualifier; vulgarity is not acceptable representation for the club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risky material is permitted, but there must be 'something there' — material should be interesting/clever rather than crude. The club does not want to be represented as vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: No condescending gestures toward the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the audience as intelligent and equal; do not signal that they 'miss' the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the hand-over-the-head gesture meaning 'it went over your heads' was cited as a huge turnoff. Belittling the audience's intelligence is a major negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based booking (no favoritism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booking decisions are based on merit, not personal relationships or favors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if someone recommends you, you must earn spots on your performance. The booker explicitly states 'I booked a show on merit, not because I like you or we had dinner yesterday.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, trusted recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to auditions typically comes through recommendations from comics who already work at the club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The booker needs someone she trusts to vouch. Bad or dishonest recommendations (recommending friends who aren't ready as a favor) are harmful: they damage the newcomer's confidence and reflect poorly on the recommender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recorded clips for scouting
rubrics_metrics.description: Online clips (e.g., YouTube) are used to quickly check a comic's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube reduces the need for physical tapes and allows one-click verification, but recorded clips do not replace the need for a trusted recommendation and live audition impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lineup balance (ethnic, gender, political variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every lineup should have balance across ethnicity, gender, and political viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She builds each show to achieve variety so audiences see a balanced bill; this is an explicit criterion when constructing shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slotting order and show prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Bigger/established comics are slotted first, then the remainder of the lineup is built around them; certain shows (e.g., Friday 6pm) receive special focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She books show by show and concentrates on priority time slots first. This logistical ordering affects who gets which stage times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to comedy as a craft ('real comics' vs 'career comics')
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for performers who remain 'comics' regardless of outside success, rather than those who treat standup as a stepping stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'real comics' include Dave Chappelle and Chris Rock who keep putting in the work. Advice to aspirants: keep writing and have passion; without passion, comedy isn't for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion for nerves but consistency in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The booker recognizes nerves (e.g., shaking hands, wet palms, crying) and is compassionate, but will not let emotional displays change her booking decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the stakes matters, but pity or sympathy does not override merit-based judgement or honest assessment of a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impression-based follow-up booking instead of formal pass/fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than a formal 'pass,' the booker forms an impression and may give a few regular spots if she sees potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If performers show promise they receive follow-up bookings; if not, she 'pulls back' — an iterative, impression-driven process rather than a binary acceptance at audition.
